papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation For Document Question Answering: A Review Of Retrieval, Embedding, Vector Search And Grounded Answer Generation
papers.abstract: Abstract—The rapid growth of digital documents creates a need for systems that can find relevant information and answer questions accurately. Traditional question-answering systems rely on predefined knowledge bases or keyword search and may fail to understand the meaning of complex questions, while large language models alone can produce fluent but unsupported answers. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines information retrieval with the generation abilities of large language models. This paper reviews RAG for document question answering. It explains sparse retrieval with BM25, dense retrieval with dual encoders and sentence embeddings, approximate nearest-neighbour vector search, re-ranking, and the integration of retrieved passages into generation, including fusion-in-decoder and self-reflective retrieval. Practical issues such as chunking, context length and the tendency of models to overlook information in the middle of long contexts are discussed, together with evaluation of faithfulness and relevance. A five-layer system is proposed in which users upload PDF documents that are extracted, cleaned and chunked, embedded with a sentence-transformer model and stored in a vector database; queries retrieve relevant chunks that are passed to an LLM to generate grounded answers through a Streamlit interface. Research gaps, objectives and a comparison of retrieval methods are presented.

papers.title: Ontology-Guided Knowledge Graph Construction and Robust Evidence Retrieval for Indian Knowledge Systems
papers.abstract: Retrieving evidence from Indian Knowledge Systems is complicated by transliteration variants, ambiguous names, and relations distributed across passages. We present an ontology-guided knowledge graph (KG) pipeline that links typed entities and relations extracted with Qwen3-32B to original textual evidence. Retrieval combines sense-aware grounding, bounded graph traversal, lexical anchors, relationship-vector search, and passage reranking. We evaluate KG alone, single-vector retrieval (SV), and KG unions with SV and Entity Notes on 320 questions from Dhara Bench, matching the per-question candidate count across internal systems under BGE and Qwen rerankers. Standalone KG has the highest Precision@5 under both rerankers and the highest MRR@20 in Counting, Composite, and Multi-hop among the evaluated internal configurations. With Qwen, KG achieves Multi-hop MRR@20 of 0.8722, compared with 0.7622 for the fully reranked KG + SV union. The KG + SV + Entity Notes union instead provides the highest overall Recall@20 (0.5134), compared with 0.4347 for KG. On the 15 Multi-hop questions, Qwen KG achieves complete-evidence MRR@20 of 0.4651 versus 0.3372 for SV, while both full unions complete ten questions within twenty results compared with nine for KG. Gemini 3.7 Flash, evaluated through manually reviewed source mappings, re mains stronger on overall MRR and nDCG, while internal systems have category-specific advantages. All comparisons are descriptive. A separate deployment timing study measures mean retrieval times of 20.374 s for KG and 0.646 s for SV. The findings support selecting KG or its unions according to the required balance of early relevance, evidence completeness, and retrieval cost.

papers.title: Function Inversion Reporting
papers.abstract: In the Function Inversion problem, the goal is to invert a function $f:[N] \to [N]$ in two phases. In the preprocessing phase, the offline algorithm computes an advice string of length $S$ bits. In the online phase, the online algorithm receives the advice and a challenge $y \in [N]$, and the goal is to find a preimage $x \in [N]$ such that $f(x) = y$ in time $T$. The problem was initially studied in cryptography, but in recent years it has found various applications to data structure problems. Yet, several of the applications require a variant of Function Inversion, known as Function Inversion Reporting, where the goal is to output all preimages of the challenge $y$. In this paper, we study the Function Inversion Reporting problem in a systematic way by unifying and improving existing algorithms. As a result, we obtain improved data structures for several problems including 3SUM-Indexing Reporting, Range Reporting, Approximate Nearest Neighbor, Jumbled Indexing Reporting, and Gapped String Indexing Reporting.

papers.title: AI Safety for AI Agents in Europe Part IV : Two Independent Checks and Endpoint-Side Reconstruction to Prevent Tool Misuse, Memory Poisoning, Unauthorized Delegation and Unlawful Data Use — Supporting EU AI Act Record-Keeping, Human Oversight and Cybersecurity, GDPR Purpose Limitation and DORA
papers.abstract: Abstract In most AI-agent and automation stacks, one component decides and a downstream component simply trusts that decision. A policy engine, gateway, classifier, trusted execution environment or approval step says yes. The tool, MCP server, database, cloud API or payment rail then carries out whatever request arrives with that approval. This leaves several gaps: the checker may be the same component that collected the inputs; approvals, tokens and receipts can be replayed, widened, rerouted or used after policy has changed; the operation that was checked can differ from the one actually committed, a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap; personal and enterprise data, once readable, can be indexed, embedded, joined, exported, used for training or used to steer an agent without any explicit authorization for that use. Under GDPR purpose limitation and the EU AI Act’s expectations for oversight and cybersecurity, these gaps are exactly where controls are needed. Today they are mostly covered by policy, logging and after-the-fact audit. This disclosure describes a two-instance execution-control architecture that removes the single point of trust: First check, at collection time. A first protected domain binds inputs, instructions, provenance, purpose, jurisdiction, scope and permitted effect when the data arrives. An input integrity gateway seals provenance first, so poisoned inputs are refused binding. Second, independent check, at execution time. A second protected domain validates the proposed action against that binding. It is independent through a separate hardware root, session, keys, runtime or administration. It produces evidence cross-committed to the binding, so neither artifact alone can authorize anything. Release only on agreement. Only when both artifacts mutually corroborate is a single-use, non-bearer authority released. The endpoint checks what is actually happening. At the execution boundary, the endpoint independently reconstructs the actual pending operation through its own attested observation channel. Endpoints include: a tool dispatcher, MCP or connector gateway, or API gateway; a database commit or cloud control plane; cross-border data egress, a payment rail or an actuator. What the endpoint reconstructs. It reconstructs recipient, purpose, jurisdiction, data category and the actual operation. It checks these against both artifacts and against its own state (nonce, counter, spent-capability, and its own policy and revocation epochs). Atomic commit. The endpoint commits the operation atomically, as exactly the operation it verified. Contained compromise. A compromise of either domain, the transport channel or the compute plane is confined to its own window and cannot by itself make an unauthorized act effective. Mismatches fail closed before the effect, not through rollback afterwards. Readable but inert data. Data, agent memories and retrieved documents can remain stored and readable while staying operationally inert. They cannot be indexed, embedded, exported, served, used for training or used to influence a tool call unless that specific use is authorized. Chained evidence. Evidence produced at the endpoint becomes a required input to the next step, and chained validation receipts provide a verifiable record at every point. Shared, not central, authority. Distributed partial shares can replace any central authority, so no single party ever holds a complete reusable authorization. The 54 claims, 15 of them independent, cover: AI-agent tool dispatch; MCP and connector supply-chain substitution; computer-use and browser actions; memory and RAG inertness; multi-agent delegation chains; autonomous cloud-control changes; regulated AI output release by purpose, jurisdiction and recipient; coding and CI/CD agents; agent skills and marketplace extensions; multimodal assistants; voice and meeting agents with consent and recording checks; agentic purchasing; persistent AI memory; workspace and scheduled agents. Readers must cross-check it against the original PCT filing on WIPO PATENTSCOPE and the official legal texts before drawing any conclusion. Technical alignment with these provisions does not itself establish regulatory compliance. The mechanisms may support objectives associated with: EU AI Act, Article 12 (record-keeping): chained, cross-committed validation receipts at each point. EU AI Act, Article 14 (human oversight): approval evidence that must corroborate an independent check, and is verified at the point of effect. EU AI Act, Article 15 (accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity): independent checks, attested reconstruction and atomic commit against manipulation between check and action. EU AI Act, general-purpose AI with systemic risk: compromise confinement and share-based authority with no single point of failure. papers.title: G-STAR: Group-Scaled Token Capacity for Deeply Compressed Autoregressive Generation
papers.abstract: Discrete autoregressive models offer a scalable framework for image generation. However, they face a fundamental trade-off: long token sequences preserve representation quality but slow generation, while aggressive spatial compression reduces representation capacity. Based on product quantization, we show that, under a fixed nominal information budget, group size should scale quadratically with the per-axis spatial compression factor. Building on this principle, we propose GSTAR, a spatial--group co-scaling framework that enables \(32\times\) and even effective \(64\times\) compression while preserving strong reconstruction, understanding, and generation performance. Since larger groups introduce intra-group dependencies that must be modeled efficiently, we analyze their impact on inference latency and generation quality and introduce a semi-autoregressive decoder that combines parallel feature computation with lightweight causal modeling. With these designs, our highly compressed models perform competitively with leading models across five representative text-to-image benchmarks (GenEval, DPG-Bench, PRISM, LongText-Bench, and Qwen-Image-Bench). At \(1024\times1024\) resolution, our model delivers a \(20\times\) speedup over prior discrete autoregressive models, generating each image in 2.5 seconds on a single NVIDIA H200. Together, these results show that highly compressed discrete representations can enable high-quality autoregressive generation at low latency.

papers.title: Dynamic Graph Indexing for Label-Filtered Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.abstract: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) over high-dimensional vectors is a core primitive in modern retrieval systems. In practice, objects are often also associated with labels (e.g., attributes or keywords), and retrieval must combine vector similarity with explicit label-based filtering, giving rise to label-filtered ANNS. This task is challenging because label filtering and ANNS favor very different index structures, selective filters fragment the admissible search space, and updates complicate index maintenance. To address these challenges, we propose DYLAN, a dynamic composite index for label-filtered ANNS supporting containment, overlap, and their conjunctions and disjunctions. DYLAN organizes label sets by shared prefixes in a frequency-ordered trie and selectively shares HNSW-style graph indices across trie-induced subsets, so that each trie region has a constant-factor covering index while each object participates in only logarithmically many indices. To mitigate fragmentation, DYLAN performs a cross-region multi-graph search that exploits ancestor-level indices as bridges between otherwise isolated trie regions. To support insertions, it adopts a threshold-based maintenance scheme that rebuilds shared indices only when necessary, yielding low amortized update cost. Extensive experiments with real data show that DYLAN consistently improves query throughput at comparable recall, by up to two orders of magnitude on challenging label-rich datasets, while retaining competitive memory, construction, and update costs.

papers.title: dNaViT: Discrete Codes are General-Purpose Visual Representations
papers.abstract: Discrete autoregressive modeling, notably through next-token prediction, has become a cornerstone of modern language models. Extending this paradigm to vision allows visual and language models to converge on a unified framework, thereby fostering shared methodology and infrastructure. This work investigates a central question: how far can a finite discrete vocabulary go in representing the richness of the visual world? We present dNaViT, a Discrete Native-resolution Vision Transformer that produces discrete visual primitives analogous to language tokens. Built upon a frozen pretrained encoder, dNaViT applies lightweight residual modulation with a dual-branch objective to inject reconstruction-aware cues into semantic features. By leveraging grouped product quantization, it scales discrete capacity without inflating spatial sequence lengths, while a balanced training recipe maintains both semantic and pixel-level information. Consequently, dNaViT functions as a versatile discrete visual tokenizer, enabling unified encoding across downstream tasks alongside high-fidelity image decoding. Extensive evaluations show that dNaViT matches or exceeds task-specific baselines across 12 visual understanding benchmarks, 4 generation benchmarks, and an image editing benchmark. These findings demonstrate that a compact discrete vocabulary can serve as a universal visual currency and unlock the full potential of fully unified, native multimodal methodology.

papers.title: Autonomous Continual Learning and Knowledge Transfer via Cortex-Inspired Neural Assemblies
papers.abstract: Unlike the brain, artificial neural networks (ANNs) suffer from "catastrophic forgetting": complete overwriting of solutions when re-training on new functions ("concept shift") or on a disjoint domain of the current function ("domain shift"). ANNs require each batch of data to be roughly representative of the complete distribution, a typically expensive and impractical requirement. In this paper, we introduce Functional Task Networks (FTNs), a method of continual learning and knowledge transfer modeled after several properties of the mammalian neocortex. FTN is formulated as a distributed, stochastic mixture of experts in which a sparse, binary routing mask is computed at inference time using a small support sample of input-output pairs. Per-batch reconfiguration of the router during training, together with mask-overlap-filtered replay, shapes a basis of overlapping, partially trained subnetworks. Unrelated tasks route through mostly separate assemblies, related tasks overlap on shared components. On block-sequentially trained continual learning and knowledge transfer tasks FTN retains solutions nearly as well as disjoint-mask isolation and attains the lowest pre-update head-start loss among matched-architecture comparators. The learned mask-overlap geometry tracks the known concept-sharing structure where available. We show experimentally that under correlated concept shift, support-set mask reconfiguration is necessary even for retention. Under domain shift, the distributed bank with replay is sufficient to handle retention without the configurer. Forward transfer, or head-start, and backward transfer, are also contributed by support-set mask configuration.

papers.title: Dhara: Evidence-Oriented Retrieval for Indian Knowledge Systems
papers.abstract: Relevant evidence in Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS) collections may be distributed across passages in different parts of a work, including verses, translations, and commentaries. Locating it requires matching natural-language questions and partially remembered verse fragments to source passages. We present Dhara, a retrieval engine combining hybrid search, chapter- and book-level Entity Notes (EN), Fuzzy Verse Retrieval (FVR), and neural reranking. Five comparisons on the 325 questions in Dhara Bench examine retrieval representations against BM25, EN's contribution, reranker quality and computation time, FVR, and Gemini. BGE-M3 single-vector retrieval exceeds BM25 in nDCG@10, Recall@20, and MRR@20 across all categories. Its scores are broadly comparable to ColBERTv2, with mean retrieval times of 0.108 s and 0.962 s under the same hardware configuration and a smaller memory footprint for chunk storage on disk. Adding EN to a direct branch with a matched candidate count improves nDCG@10 in all twelve categories with Qwen and ten with BGE; the combined ranking is capped at the same candidate count. Qwen improves nDCG@10, Precision@5, and MRR@20 over BGE in every category, at approximately 6.72 times the overall estimated serial computation time. FVR increases Verse-category nDCG@10 by approximately 20 percentage points with either reranker. Gemini is evaluated after source mapping and manual review with relevance annotations visible. The Qwen pipeline with EN and FVR has higher Recall@20 than Gemini in ten categories and stronger complete-evidence retrieval in Multi-hop questions, while Gemini retains early-relevance advantages in several categories. The results inform retrieval choices according to evidence requirements and resource budgets.

papers.title: Neural Activity Synchronization-Based Fast Local Learnable Spiking Neural Network Architecture
papers.abstract: Implementing intelligent learning systems on low- power edge devices is challenging due to the high compu- tational complexity, training latency, and energy demands of traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), biologically plausible and spike-driven, come as an alternative. However, SNN training commonly relies on backpropagation through time (BPTT), which is computationally expensive, inherently global, and unsuitable for battery-driven devices. This work proposes a novel local learning framework for multi-layered SNNs inspired by Neural Activity Synchronization (NAS). Each layer updates its own weights using locally com- puted gradients. No gradient backpropagation is needed. This significantly reduces computational complexity, training latency, and energy consumption. The proposed SNN model is trained and evaluated on the MNIST dataset, achieving a classification accuracy of 97.78%. The model is also analyzed with Gaussian and salt-and-pepper noise, demonstrating robust performance across different noise levels.

papers.title: Hybrid Product Search Without the Copy: Lexical, Semantic and Filtered Retrieval Served Directly from a Data Lake
papers.abstract: E-commerce catalogs increasingly live in lakehouse tables: Apache Iceberg metadata over Parquet files in object storage. Product search, however, still runs on copies of that catalog, in a lexical engine and a vector database, each with its own ingestion pipeline, schema, staleness window and bill. We show that search applications can be hosted directly on the data lake, with the lakehouse table as the single system of record. We extend Apache Pinot, a real-time OLAP engine that already serves Iceberg tables in place, with BM25 relevance scoring over its Lucene text index, corpus-wide term statistics so that scores are comparable across files, and reciprocal rank fusion in plain SQL; a real-time table fed by a stream can sit behind the same table, merged by the broker. On the Amazon ESCI benchmark (1.2M US products, 22,458 test queries), hybrid search served from the lake matches exact retrieval (nDCG@10 .361). The lake table is queryable 149 s after its files are registered, and a lake commit is searchable in 3.8 s, close to indexing directly into a search engine. On a brand-sorted lake of 277M products (0.8 TB), one 16-vCPU node answers brand-scoped vector, BM25 and client-fused hybrid searches in 6.5-9 ms (p50), sustains 1,100 vector and 635 BM25 searches per second at under 180 ms p99, and makes a commit searchable in 4.3 s. papers.title: MV-IVF: Multi-Vector Retrieval via Multi-Vector Clustering
papers.abstract: Multi-vector retrieval represents each query and document as a set of embeddings and scores relevance via fine-grained set-to-set interactions such as MaxSim (Chamfer similarity). This expressiveness improves retrieval quality over single-vector representations, but makes search substantially more expensive. Existing systems address this challenge primarily through proxy representations or filter-and-rerank pipelines that reduce candidate generation to single-vector search. We study the complementary direction of building a native IVF-style index directly over multi-vector data. We introduce MV-IVF, an inverted-file index for multi-vector retrieval built on MV-Lloyd, a new Lloyd-style algorithm for clustering point clouds under a Chamfer objective. Our key observation is that once point clouds are assigned to clusters, the center-update step reduces to standard single-vector clustering over the flattened embeddings in each cluster. This enables efficient construction of a hierarchical IVF tree with center point clouds at internal nodes. At query time, MV-IVF performs best-first beam search over the tree to identify promising leaf clusters, then scores the documents in those leaves. We further accelerate search using low-bit quantization, query compression, and cache-efficient batched search. We implement MV-IVF in MVSIC, an optimized C++ library and unified evaluation framework for multi-vector retrieval that includes several major approaches. Across BEIR and LoTTE text retrieval benchmarks, MV-IVF achieves strong latency--recall tradeoffs, the best batched throughput frontiers, and favorable build-time and index-size profiles. At $90\%$ Recall-$10$@$10$, MV-IVF achieves up to $8.03\times$ lower single-query latency and up to $173.5\times$ higher QPS than the baselines, demonstrating that native IVF-style indexing is practical and effective for scalable multi-vector retrieval.

papers.title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Knowledge Graphs: A Review
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can produce fluent but factually incorrect statements, known as hallucinations, which limits their reliability in healthcare, law, education and other critical domains. This paper reviews methods that reduce hallucination by grounding generation in external knowledge. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) retrieves relevant passages at query time and conditions the model on them, while Knowledge Graphs (KGs) provide structured, verifiable facts and explicit relations that support multi-hop reasoning. The review explains dense passage retrieval, retrieval-augmented pre-training, graph-based RAG that summarizes communities of related entities, and reasoning that walks over knowledge-graph paths. It also covers evaluation, including truthfulness benchmarks and metrics for faithfulness, context relevance and answer relevance. A hybrid architecture is proposed that combines vector retrieval with knowledge-graph lookup, assembles grounded context, generates answers with citations and verifies claims before responding. Research gaps, objectives, a comparison of grounding strategies and challenges such as retrieval errors, outdated knowledge, graph construction cost and latency are discussed. The review concludes that combining unstructured retrieval with structured knowledge offers a practical route to more accurate and transparent LLM applications.

papers.title: Per-Query Recall Guarantees for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in Dynamic Vector Databases
papers.abstract: Vector search runs as an operator in database systems, where a missed neighbor can make a filter, join, or aggregate wrong, yet approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes are tuned only for an average recall target. In our measurements, indexes tuned to an average recall of 0.99 left 5-19% of in-distribution queries and, tuned without a query log, up to 99.6% of real out-of-distribution queries below this target, and the misses grew under updates. We present PQR-Search, a k-ANN search method that guarantees $\Pr[\mathrm{Recall}(q)<τ]\leδ$ for every query. The probability is only over a random orthogonal transformation inside the index, so no distributional assumption is needed, only that queries and updates do not depend on it; the guarantee holds after insertions and deletions without retuning. PQR-Search stores 1-bit codes of rotated residuals with respect to IVF centroids and prunes with exact quantiles of their error distribution. A formula predicting the fraction of vectors that pass the code test, with no data-fitted constants, chooses index parameters and maintenance operations without affecting the guarantee. On 20 datasets of up to 100 million vectors, failure rates stayed at most $δ$ in every audit, including all 33 steps of the official NeurIPS'23 streaming runbook, whereas CTR, a conformal guarantee averaged over queries, left up to 16.4% of queries below the target. Where HNSW tuned to an average recall of 0.99 met that target, PQR-Search had 2.5x its single-query latency and 1.3x lower batch throughput, yet that HNSW still left 3-29% of queries below 0.99. PQR-Search was faster than FAISS exhaustive search in every static setting (26.4x geometric mean in batch; 69-154x at 100M scale), faster than IVF with nprobe chosen afterwards for every test query in all 52 main settings, and 27-76x faster at one thread than PUFFINN, which also gives per-query guarantees.

papers.abstract: We present \textsc{Ginger}, a state-of-the-art open-source C++ library for graph-based approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS). We developed \textsc{Ginger} at Google to push the speed and memory efficiency of graph search on large and high-dimensional embedding datasets. \textsc{Ginger} surpasses existing ANNS libraries with regards to query throughput and indexing time while matching the memory footprint of the most space-efficient competitors. \textsc{Ginger} builds upon recent advances in proximity graph construction (PiPNN) and vector quantization (TurboQuant). We introduce Nested TurboQuant (NTQ), a two-level quantizer which supports low precision graph navigation and high precision reranking in a single code. This representation achieves near floating point precision with $2.6\times$ less memory. We also compress the size of our proximity graphs by up to $2.5\times$ without impacting query throughput. We combine graph reordering with a new lossless compression codec called AdaptiveGap, which builds upon StreamVByte. At $95\%$ recall, \textsc{Ginger} speeds up query throughput by an average of $1.8\times$ over each dataset's fastest competitor and by at least $2.3\times$ over any single library. This lead grows to $2.9\times$ over compact libraries on high-dimensional embeddings.

papers.title: Sharp Limits of Graph-Based Nearest Neighbor Search on the Sphere
papers.abstract: We study the degree needed for greedy graph search to find the exact nearest neighbor from every starting point on graphs of $n$ independent data points on the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^d$. For uniform data, we determine an explicit sublinear degree threshold when $d$ is proportional to $\log n$, and the threshold $2^{d/2+o(d)}$ in the dense regime $\sqrt{\log n}\ll d\ll\log n$. Above these thresholds by fixed exponent gaps, the nearest-neighbor graph succeeds from every entry for most uniform queries with high probability, with evaluation cost on the same exponential scale as its degree. Matching lower bounds hold for every graph designed after observing the sample. For nonuniform data in the dense regime, local density variation shifts the critical degree. Under explicit local regularity conditions and within a specified range of density variation, we derive a sharp worst-case degree curve and show that the nearest-neighbor graph attains it. We construct sampling densities and query distributions for which, with high probability, every graph whose degree lies below this curve by a fixed exponent gap has failing entries for most queries. Allowing fresh uniform random entries reduces the cost of exact recovery. For uniform data in the dense regime, we determine the exact exponent for the number of distinct distance evaluations over a range of degrees below the critical threshold. Independent restarts on a single graph joining points within a prescribed radius attain this exponent with high probability. Matching lower bounds hold for adaptive local exploration on threshold and nearest-neighbor graphs using entries independent of the data. Optimizing within this degree range lowers the exponent from $\frac12\log2\approx0.347$ for success from every entry to approximately $0.243$.

papers.title: ArcadeDB in Python: An In-Process Multi-Model Database
papers.abstract: Some Python workflows need transactional reads and writes over documents, traversals over a graph, and similarity search over vector embeddings. In practice these are split across separate systems (a document store, a graph engine, and a vector index), and the data is copied between them and kept consistent by application code. ArcadeDB is an open-source multi-model database engine, written in Java, that supports all three access patterns and can be embedded in a host process. We present arcadedb-embedded, a Python package that runs ArcadeDB inside the Python process via JPype, using a Java Runtime Environment bundled in the wheel. One pip install gives a database with documents, a property graph, and vector search, and needs no Java installation. Query results can be returned as Python lists, NumPy arrays, pandas DataFrames, or Arrow tables. We demonstrate a hybrid retrieval workflow that chains vector search, SQL filtering, and graph traversal over one dataset. We benchmark arcadedb-embedded against SQLite, DuckDB, LadybugDB, and Chroma, and report its costs.

papers.title: A Local-First AI/ML Intelligence Layer for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in a Spring Boot Application
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong generative capability but suffer from hallucination, stale knowledge, and an inability to cite sources. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates these weaknesses by grounding responses in externally retrieved documents. This paper presents the design and implementation of an AI/ML intelligence layer that integrates RAG into an existing Spring Boot / Kotlin application with minimal new infrastructure. The layer reuses the application's embedded SQLite database as a vector store, serialises embedding vectors as little-endian BLOBs, and performs brute-force cosine-similarity search in process. A local, Docker-native Ollama runtime provides both the embedding model (nomic-embed-text) and the generative model (llama3.2), eliminating external API keys. We describe the layered architecture, the ingestion and query pipelines, the data model, tenant-scoped security, and deployment topology, and we discuss the scalability and quality trade-offs of the local-first approach. The result is a reference pattern for adding private, citeable, document-grounded chat to conventional enterprise web stacks without adopting a heavyweight vector database or third-party LLM subscription.

papers.title: Automated Resume Screening System
papers.abstract: - Many automated applicant-screening tools depend on word overlap, so they cannot see that two differently phrased resumes may describe the same expertise, and they return scores that neither recruiters nor candidates are able to examine. This paper presents an open-source, explainable hybrid framework for resume screening that runs on ordinary CPUs. Uploaded PDF, DOCX or plain-text files are cleaned and parsed, extracted skills are converted to standard labels, and a lightweight sentence encoder places the resume and the job posting in one shared 384-dimensional vector space. The overall job-fit value blends semantic similarity, skill coverage and an experience adjustment, and an extended profile also takes project and education relevance into account. Each matched skill is linked to a supporting sentence in the resume, a presentation-quality index is computed separately from job fit, rule-based integrity checks flag questionable content, and a vector database supports semantic retrieval and near-duplicate detection. The paper states the scoring model and the processing algorithm, outlines the relational and vector storage layers, and summarizes the functional checks carried out in an implementation audit. The audit also exposed open problems, chiefly fixed weights, integrity results that are not stored, missing access control and the lack of a dispute mechanism; these are reported openly, together with a reproducible protocol for assessing ranking quality

papers.title: Turbocharging PiPNN for Proximity and $k$-NN Graph Building
papers.abstract: Graph-based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) indexes such as HNSW and Vamana deliver state-of-the-art query performance at the cost of large indexing times. The recently introduced PiPNN method drastically accelerated index construction by way of a partitioning-based algorithm leveraging dense matrix multiplication and top-$K$ aggregation kernels. In this paper, we unlock the full potential of PiPNN's hardware-friendly algorithm design. We introduce PiPNN II, which optimizes multiple steps of the PiPNN recipe, giving up to $8\times$ speedups for graph-based ANNS index construction. In addition, we present GPiPNN, a GPU implementation which builds comparable ANNS indices up to $43.7\times$ faster than Jasper and up to $50\times$ faster than CAGRA. We also extend PiPNN II and GPiPNN to compute high-quality $k$-NN graphs directly, which unlocks massive speedups over methods used in many existing systems for clustering, anomaly detection, and more. For 10-NN graph building at $90\%$ recall, we obtain up to a $13\times$ speedup on CPUs and $6.6\times$ on GPUs as compared to the prior best methods. PiPNN II can build a billion-scale 10-NN graph in under 16 minutes. Common to both PiPNN II and GPiPNN is the use of quantization to reduce memory traffic and leverage fast low-precision matrix operations. Top-$K$ emerges as a new bottleneck, which we optimize with specialized code for specific $K$, and by fusing with the matrix kernel to avoid materializing the distance matrix to memory. On CPUs, we demonstrate further performance improvements by leveraging our matrix kernels in the RobustPrune procedure proposed in Vamana and used in PiPNN. On GPUs, we flatten recursive partitioning into segmented batches, use one fused top-$K$ abstraction for partitioning and leaf scoring, and prune with already-witnessed direct edges rather than new candidate-to-candidate scoring passes.

papers.title: FlyHash for LLM Agent Memory: An Empirical Validation and a New Application
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory stores to retain information across conversations, typically via dense vector embeddings searched with approximate nearest-neighbor methods. The fruit fly's olfactory circuit computes a locality-sensitive hash of sensory input using a strikingly different mechanism - sparse random projection followed by winner-take-all competition - and prior work (Dasgupta et al., 2017) showed this scheme, dubbed FlyHash, preserves neighbor structure better per bit than conventional random-hyperplane hashing (SimHash) on several benchmarks. We apply FlyHash, to our knowledge for the first time, to LLM agent memory retrieval, and ask three questions a practitioner actually needs answered: does the quality advantage hold under a correctly matched-bit protocol (it does, robustly, across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, with one specific, previously undocumented comparison pitfall identified and corrected along the way); does that advantage translate into real memory and latency savings, including against the dense-vector indexing (HNSW) practitioners default to today (no: at equal bits FlyHash's codes are larger and slower to compare than SimHash's, and HNSW dominates both hash methods at ordinary scale; a sparse-set comparison we introduce recovers most but not all of a naive latency gap, leaving hashing's practical case narrower and more specific than the quality result alone implies); and does the advantage survive genuine, non-circular agent-memory relevance labels rather than the nearest-neighbor-by-embedding proxy this literature otherwise relies on (it does). We report all three answers precisely, including the two that narrow rather than flatter the headline result, and release our implementation, a working agent-memory demo, and a full account of the methodological pitfalls we found and corrected.

papers.title: Modular and Efficient Approximate Nearest Neighbors Search with Vectorium and kANNolo
papers.abstract: Approximate Nearest Neighbors (ANN) search over neural embeddings powers modern retrieval systems such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Embeddings come in three representations (dense, sparse and multi-vector), and efficient search combines an index structure, a similarity function and a quantization scheme. Existing libraries fix one combination, hard-code each one separately, or factor only one side of the problem, and none covers all three representations. We present Vectorium and kANNolo, two open-source Rust libraries that split this design space into a data-management layer and an indexing layer. Vectorium abstracts the vector, the distance function, the quantizer and the dataset independently, and provides 11 encoders, from 32-bit floats to sub-bit codes. On top of it, kANNolo implements Hierarchical Navigable Small-World (HNSW) graph and Inverted Vector File (IVF) indexes that are generic over representation, encoder and metric, and a two-stage index that composes any first-stage index with any rescoring dataset. Since every combination is specialized at compile time, this modularity adds no run-time overhead, and the resulting indexes reach state-of-the-art performance: our Product Quantization matches Faiss in accuracy at competitive speed, our RaBitQ and HNSW match or outperform their reference implementations, and our IVF outperforms Faiss. Against six dense and five sparse systems on seven public collections, our indexes give the best memory-throughput trade-off on dense data in 9 of 12 collection-accuracy pairs and perform well on out-of-distribution queries. On sparse data, the systems built on Vectorium lead on all three collections, with Seismic and SeismicWave the fastest and kANNolo's indexes the most compact.

papers.title: O2N2: Efficient Doubly Oblivious Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.abstract: Privacy-preserving approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search allows clients to search from an untrusted server without revealing sensitive queries, and is useful in scenarios like medical diagnostics and credit scoring. Among the various privacy-preserving primitives, trusted execution environments (TEEs) have much lower overhead than heavy cryptographic ones, yet they leak memory access patterns, enabling adversaries to infer query contents. Oblivious RAM (ORAM) can be used to hide those access patterns at $\mathrm{O}(\log N)$ asymptotic cost, but existing high-performance ANN search algorithms (e.g., IVF or HNSW) exhibit complex, data-dependent access patterns that are unfriendly for ORAM. Furthermore, standard ORAM constructions typically assume there exists a small amount of trusted storage, which weakens the security guarantees and is not always feasible. Solutions that eliminate such trusted storage (known as {\em double obliviousness}) typically degrade performance further to $\mathrm{O}(\log^2 N)$. We introduce O2N2, a doubly oblivious ANN framework built around single-path search in randomly rotated $k$-d tree forests. A pointer-based Circuit ORAM stores the search structure, with separate storage for compact internal nodes and vector-bearing leaves. Each visited leaf is processed by an oblivious selection network, and fixed-schedule duplicate removal and selection combine the local results into the final top-$k$. We evaluate O2N2 on real-world datasets and further test its scalability on 100 million vectors. For 10-NN and 100-NN search at the specified high-recall targets, it achieves a $9.8$--$125.9\times$ speedup over the fastest doubly oblivious baselines.

Among the various privacy-preserving primitives, trusted execution environments (TEEs) have much lower overhead than heavy cryptographic ones, yet they leak memory access patterns, enabling adversaries to infer query contents. Oblivious RAM (ORAM) can be used to hide those access patterns at $\mathrm{O}(\log N)$ asymptotic cost, but existing high-performance ANN search algorithms (e.g., IVF or HNSW) exhibit complex, data-dependent access patterns that are unfriendly for ORAM.
innovations: We introduce O2N2, a doubly oblivious ANN framework built around single-path search in randomly rotated $k$-d tree forests.

papers.title: Federated Vector Retrieval across Heterogeneous VectorDBs
papers.abstract: Vector databases are now core infrastructure for AI retrieval systems, yet many real deployments must serve queries over multiple independently constructed vectorDBs built with different embedding models. This creates a systems problem of federated retrieval over heterogeneous vectorDBs: vectors and similarity scores are not directly comparable across embedding spaces, while fully resolving this incompatibility through corpus-wide re-embedding and re-indexing is often operationally prohibitive. Existing methods therefore face a difficult trade-off between retrieval quality, construction cost, and query throughput. We present HVMap, a lightweight compatibility layer for federated retrieval across heterogeneous vectorDBs. Instead of rebuilding databases into a unified space, HVMap learns bidirectional mappings between embedding spaces using a fuzzy contrastive loss, enabling calibrated cross-database scoring without corpus migration or index reconstruction. HVMap is system-agnostic and further scales to multi-vectorDB settings while preserving ranking fidelity through a hub-based architecture. We evaluate HVMap in open-domain, cross-domain, and scale-out settings, and also construct a new benchmark for heterogeneous cross-domain federation. Across these settings, HVMap consistently achieves a better quality--cost--throughput trade-off than baselines, achieving up to 3.59X higher nDCG@10, up to 2.01X higher query throughput, and construction time as low as 0.3% of baseline methods. These results show that HVMap makes heterogeneous vectorDB federation practical at scale.

papers.title: Recast: Refinement-Centered Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Optimized for Storage
papers.abstract: Large-scale ANNS systems often exploit storage in addition to DRAM for supporting vector search. The central question is how to divide the work between memory and storage for achieving both high query throughput-recall and good index maintenance performance. Existing storage-optimized ANNS paradigms fall short of providing a complete answer: disk-resident graph indexes have difficulty in supporting efficient vector deletions, while posting-list systems often incur more disk I/Os for queries. In this paper, we introduce a refinement-centered paradigm for storage-optimized ANNS systems. We propose Recast as a concrete design of this paradigm. Recast stores raw vectors on disk and keeps an IVF index with our RecastQ quantization encoding in memory. For an ANNS query, Recast selects nprobe inverted lists and performs SIMD-based FastScan on their RecastQ codes to identify refinement candidates in memory. It then retrieves candidate vectors from disk, computes exact distances, and refines the top-K result. To reduce disk I/Os, RecastQ computes uncertainty intervals containing true distances with high probability. Our QUIC policy selects a minimal refinement set based on these intervals, minimizing candidate-retrieval I/Os. Both the on-disk raw vectors and the in-memory IVF structure support insertions and deletions. Experiments on real-world data sets show that Recast processes batched insertions and deletions 3.10-37.27x faster than SPFresh and OdinANN, while its QPS at 0.99 recall changes by at most 6.9% after updating 50% of the corpus. For static queries at 0.99 recall, Recast achieves 1.56-2.01x the QPS of the strongest baseline with the matched memory budget on each data set, while requiring 1.22-6.75x less external storage than the evaluated systems. At matched in-memory space, RecastQ also provides a better Recall-refinement frontier than RaBitQ.

papers.title: OctEx: Billion-Scale Vector Search by Precomputed Lattice Neighbor Lists on GPUs
papers.abstract: Approximate nearest-neighbor search on GPUs serves retrieval-augmented generation, recommendation, and deduplication over datasets of up to billions of vectors. The fastest GPU indexes at high recall, such as CAGRA, walk proximity graphs in chained rounds, each of which waits for the distances of the previous one. High recall therefore costs many dependent rounds per query. Our insight is to spend the HBM of the GPUs on precomputed neighbor lists, so that a query reads its candidates in one parallel step instead of a chain of rounds. This paper turns the above insight into a GPU vector search system, namely OctEx, which holds hundreds of randomly projected copies of the dataset in GPU memory. Every copy rounds its vectors to the nearest points of a regular grid whose cells are nearly round and stores for every populated cell the list of vectors nearest to its center. A query reads the lists of its cells in all copies at once and then, in a fixed number of waves, the precomputed neighbor lists of its best hits. OctEx ranks the union of all hits by an int8 sketch before one exact rerank. OctEx runs the whole search of a batch as CUDA graphs over all GPUs of a server and places every part of its index in HBM or host memory by its access frequency. On four H100 GPUs at recall 0.95 to 0.995, OctEx outperforms CAGRA by 2.0x to 46.4x on seven datasets of up to one hundred million vectors, and by 1.46x to 2.05x on the one billion vectors of Deep1B and SIFT1B, whose indexes it builds in 44 to 47 minutes. OctEx also outperforms GGNN, PathWeaver, FlowANN, and the cuVS inverted file indexes IVF-PQ and IVF-RaBitQ by 5.4x to 343x.

papers.title: Nonreciprocal Spherical Attention and Retrieval: Sharp Coarsening Clocks and Certified Score Correction
papers.abstract: We develop nonreciprocal spherical attention as a mathematical framework for coarsening and compressed nearest-neighbor retrieval. For two shrinking acute blocks whose centers have zero skew pairing and whose total mass ratio is subexponential in inverse temperature, we prove $\lim_{β\to\infty}β^{-1}\log T_β=1-\cosφ$, without restricting particle-count growth. An explicit three-body flow has two rigorously separated metastable exponents. For finite compression, mass centering yields a sharp $O(r^2)$ attention-output error bound at fixed temperature, with an explicit spherical-normalization correction. We formulate skew query-side score calibration as a strictly convex moment problem and derive a unique normal equation, residual-based optimization certificates, and bounded low-rank projections. A norm-aware margin objective calibrates native squared-distance rankings. Experiments use semantic retrieval data, one million visual descriptors with three codebook seeds, and a ten-million-vector FAISS IVF-PQ index with recomputed exact cosine ground truth. On SIFT1M, skew margin calibration raises native-L2 hit@10 from 0.8926 to 0.8948; symmetric calibration reaches 0.8996. The ten-million-vector index reaches 0.8827 hit@10 at 0.1794 ms per query in a four-thread batch benchmark, while validation selects no skew update. Exact streamed attention over ten million keys evaluates compressed memory on 1,024 held-out queries. Independent matrix solves, automatic differentiation, finite differences, interval arithmetic, full-flow tests, and nine Rocq-checked algebra lemmas support reproducibility. Directionality alone does not establish retrieval superiority.

papers.title: The Tangled Web They Weave: Exploring Neural Representations with Directed Simplicial Complexes
papers.abstract: Understanding how artificial neural networks (ANNs) represent and combine features internally is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Existing neural circuit-discovery methods represent neuron interactions as pairwise edges in a graph. But distributed neural representations consist of large groups of neurons that are inherently linked by higher-order causal dependencies: suppressing a subgroup of neurons in concert may shift the activation of other neurons in the feature representation. We propose a method to construct filtered directed simplicial complexes (DSCs) that give a topological representation of such dependencies, built from the activation profiles of an ANN on a given set of inputs. Our approach treats ANNs as structural causal models and uses counterfactual ablations to test for causal links between groups of internal neurons within specific input contexts. As a proof of concept, we apply the approach to a pair of small multilayer perceptron (MLP) architectures in a synthetic two-dimensional quadrant classification task. In these examples, DSCs recover the designed feature pathways and coordinated class transitions, and the complexes of trained networks are higher-dimensional than those of their handcrafted references. As validation, we compare our method with graph-based circuit-discovery baselines and find that their 1-skeletons agree within the relations that a weight graph can represent. These results support DSCs as context-dependent descriptions of multi-neuron computation and may thus provide a novel, orthogonal framework to study the phenomenon of distributed feature representations and polysemanticity.

papers.title: Implicit Additively Weighted Geodesic Voronoi Diagrams and Applications
papers.abstract: Let $P$ be a simple polygon with $m$ vertices. After $O(m)$-time preprocessing of $P$, for any set $S$ of $n$ additively weighted point sites, we compute an implicit additively weighted geodesic Voronoi diagram in $O(n\log n+n\log^2 m)$ time, supporting nearest-neighbor queries in $O(\log(n+m))$ time. In contrast, explicitly constructing the diagram requires $Ω(m)$ time. Our algorithm introduces a new sweep-line paradigm that avoids explicitly constructing the diagram, together with a novel technique for point location in implicit subdivisions. As applications, we obtain new dynamic data structures for additively weighted geodesic nearest-neighbor searching and the first efficient algorithms for shortest paths in geodesic disk graphs. After the same $O(m)$-time preprocessing, single-source shortest paths in a geodesic disk graph of $n$ sites can be computed in $O(n\log n+n\log^2 m)$ time in the unweighted case and $O(n^{3/2}(\log n+\log^2 m))$ time in the weighted case. We also extend our techniques to implicit farthest geodesic Voronoi diagrams for unweighted sites, obtaining analogous bounds and dynamic farthest-neighbor data structures.

papers.title: Fidelity Synopses: Pre-Execution Plan Selection for Approximate Vector Search
papers.abstract: Vector search has become a database operator with many physical implementations: different index families, build-time and search-time parameters, and compressed or disk-resident variants. Each trades cost against fidelity, the fraction of a query's exact top-k nearest neighbors that a configuration returns. Deployments nevertheless choose one configuration offline and use it for every query, so they are sized for their hardest queries and overpay for the rest. On a 5.8M-item LAION benchmark with four embedding models, running each query on the cheapest configuration that suffices for it would roughly halve the cost in a typical setting. Exploiting this requires predicting each configuration's fidelity before running it, which is hard because fidelity is defined by the very exact search that approximate indexes avoid. Relational optimizers solve the analogous problem for cardinality with offline synopses; we propose one for vector search. A fidelity synopsis divides the embedding space into cells around a set of landmarks and records, for every cell and configuration, how often that configuration met a fidelity target on a sample of queries. At query time, one nearest-landmark lookup yields a calibrated estimate for every configuration, and an optimizer chooses configurations so that the workload misses the target no more often than its requirement allows. We test the two premises the synopsis relies on, that fidelity varies smoothly across the embedding space and that its loss is specific to each configuration. Held to the same requirement a static deployment is built to meet, synopsis-guided selection lowers cost in all 16 combinations of model and query direction, to a median of 0.72x the static deployment, with a batched lookup of 21-32 microseconds per query. The saving persists against the best static choice among the same indexes, and within a single index at no extra memory.

papers.title: Lifelong Memory Architectures for Large Language Model Based Generative AI Systems: A Survey and Comparative Analysis
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) form the basis of multiple generative applications today, but these systems are mostly stateless which means that information keeps outside the context window disappears when the session is closed. Such limitations complicate personalization, make it difficult to maintain consistency over long interactions, and prevent the AI system from learning from its experience. Lifelong memory architectures address this problem by providing the LLM with an external, permanent memory that also includes means of information writing, retrieval, updating, consolidating, and forgetting without the need to retrain the model itself. This paper presents an overview of the developments in this area starting from early external-memory enhancement and reflective generative agents, and continuing with memory operating system, graph-shaped memory, and reinforcement learning of agent memory. We summarize our results, suggesting an operation-centered classification of such systems and compare such twelve representations with regard to scalability, retrieval efficiency, personalization, computational cost, and adaptability, discussing necessary technologies such as embeddings, approximate nearest neighbor index, knowledge graph, and retrieval-augmented generation.

papers.title: Autonomous Multi-Facet Repository Comprehension Using Hierarchical Retrieval and Cascading Multi-LLM Routing
papers.abstract: Joining unfamiliar software projects forces developers to spend days deciphering complex codebases, API routes, and runtime flows. Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines should help, but they break down on source code in practice. New engineers rarely know what specific questions to ask, and standard chunking blindly slices code mid-function. To solve these issues without manual intervention, we present RepoInsight, an end-to-end system that automatically generates an 11-facet architectural report directly from a GitHub repository URL without requiring human queries. To preserve enclosing syntax without inflating prompt token volume, RepoInsight implements hierarchical parent-child retrieval: granular 500-character child chunks are embedded via Cohere (384 dimensions) and indexed in PostgreSQL pgvector, while complete parent source files are retrieved dynamically through single batched relational queries. To control inference latency and avoid rate limits, the system applies order-preserving file deduplication to consolidate 11 architectural facets into 7 batched prompts. Generation routes through a three-tier fallback hierarchy (Groq -> Gemini 1.5 Flash -> Cohere Command-R) paired with regular-expression JSON sanitization. Empirical evaluations across seven benchmark repositories show that RepoInsight reduces redundant prompt tokens by an average of 40.2%, accelerates nearest-neighbor vector retrieval by 16.1x via HNSW graph indexing, and achieves 100% request completion under severe upstream throttling where single-provider baselines crash on 63.6% of queries. This architecture offers a practical, high-throughput foundation for automated developer onboarding. papers.title: KITE: Retrieval as a Decision Procedure for Long-Term Conversational Memory
papers.abstract: Many long-term memory systems for LLM agents are built around embedding-based retrieval. Al- though effective for semantic matching, similarity ranking alone does not establish whether re- trieved memories satisfy the conditions implied by a question. In this paper, we introduce KITE (Knowledge-Indexed Temporal Evidence), a vector-free framework that formulates memory re- trieval as an explicit decision procedure. KITE organizes multi-session conversations as structured knowledge indexed by a governed topic vocabulary, which evolves through controlled expansion and consolidation. At query time, questions are compiled into inspectable retrieval plans over the same knowledge index that guides memory construction. The plans are then executed through fixed lookup and ranking operations, while sparse lexical retrieval recovers surface details omitted from the structured representation. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S show that KITE achieves 93.5% and 86.0% accuracy while using only about 1.6k reader-context tokens per ques- tion. These results demonstrate that conversational memory can move beyond similarity ranking by unifying memory construction and query compilation around a governed index, turning retrieval into an inspectable decision procedure for determining which evidence satisfies the question.

papers.title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. We describe RAGFlow's pipeline and harness (open source at https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow), which turns the loop into five disciplined stations and keeps the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set; together they form an agent-native database: a store that hands the agent compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.

papers.title: A Provenance-Aware Framework for Cross-Modal Knowledge Discovery from Text, Images, and Audio-Visual Dialogue
papers.abstract: A large share of institutional and educational knowledge is not stored as clean digital text but is embedded in scanned documents, photographed whiteboards, signage, and recorded human dialogue such as lectures, interviews, and meetings. Classical Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD) and text-mining pipelines do not extend directly to this material, and independent single-modality pipelines cannot recognize that a fact appearing in both an image and a spoken utterance is one fact rather than two. This paper presents a provenance-aware framework for knowledge discovery from text, images, and audio-visual dialogue. The framework extracts candidate entity and relation mentions from each modality using established open-source components (scene-text detection, optical character recognition, object detection, automatic speech recognition, speaker diarization, and transformer-based language understanding), represents them under a common mention schema, and aligns them across modalities through a weighted combination of temporal, semantic, and contextual evidence. A confidence-aware fusion step merges corroborating mentions, explicitly flags conflicting evidence instead of silently overwriting it, and persists each reconciled fact in a knowledge graph whose edges carry their source modality, source segment, and fused confidence as queryable properties. A hybrid retrieval workflow combining dense vector search with graph traversal supports semantic search, summarization, and question answering with traceable evidence. We describe the architecture, the data contracts, the alignment and fusion procedures, and a component- and system-level evaluation protocol for the prototype.

papers.title: UFDR Agent: An AI-Driven Framework for Automated Analysis of Universal Forensic Extraction Device Reports in Digital Forensic Investigations
papers.abstract: Universal Forensic Extraction Device Report (UFDR) files generated from seized smartphones and computers routinely contain gigabytes to multiple terabytes of chats, call logs, images, videos and metadata, and manually reviewing this volume of evidence can take investigators weeks per device. This paper presents UFDR Agent, an AI-based analysis platform designed to automate the ingestion, structuring and querying of UFDR data using a combination of natural-language processing, computer vision and vector-similarity search. The system parses heterogeneous UFDR exports into a canonical relational schema, applies large-language-model-based intent detection to translate an investigator’s questions into structured queries, and uses vision-language and face-detection models to caption, tag and embed image evidence (and, prospectively, video) for semantic retrieval. Entity-extraction and link-analysis modules surface cryptocurrency addresses, international phone numbers, URLs and suspicious keywords, and the platform is designed to produce structured, court-oriented summary reports with timelines and an audit trail. A working prototype ingests approximately 8,900 records in 30 seconds and answers structured queries in under one second on commodity, offline hardware. This paper describes the motivation, related work, system architecture, implementation and evaluation of the proposed platform, and discusses its feasibility, expected impact on investigation timelines, and directions for future development.

papers.title: CAREERPILOT AI
papers.abstract: The increasing competition in the employment market has created significant challenges for students and job seekers in preparing effective resumes, identifying relevant skills, and performing effectively in interviews. Existing career-support systems commonly address individual tasks such as resume screening, job recommendation, or interview preparation, while providing limited integration and personalization. This paper proposes CareerPilot AI, an intelligent career assistance system that integrates resume analysis, Applicant Tracking System evaluation, job-description matching, skill-gap identification, AI-based mock interviews, response evaluation, and personalized learning-roadmap generation. The proposed system uses Natural Language Processing, Large Language Models, semantic matching, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation to process user information and generate context-aware recommendations. A web-based architecture using Streamlit and FastAPI or Flask is proposed, with PDF parsing libraries for resume extraction and vector databases for retrieval-based services. The evaluation framework measures resume parsing accuracy, resume-job matching performance, skill-gap identification, interview-response evaluation, response time, and usability. The system is designed to provide an integrated digital career mentor that connects a candidate's current profile with target job requirements and subsequent preparation activities. Actual experimental results will be obtained after implementation and testing.

papers.title: An Explainable Multi-Agent System for Real-Time SMS Smishing Detection with LangGraph Orchestration
papers.abstract: SMS has become a target for cyberattacks. Users may get one-time passwords, transaction notifications, banking alerts and other service announcements.These messages can be quite familiar, urgent, making it difficult to determine fake messages, putting users at risk of being victims of smishing. Once successful, information and authentication credentials can be stolen from victims.Current defenses are typically designed with static rules or individual AI models. They struggle to catch evolving scam messages. They also lack real-time analysis, a combined threat check and clear reasons for why a message's dangerous. To solve these problems we introduce ScamShield AI. ScamShield AI is a multi-agent AI system that works in time to detect smishing. It contains three agents: an OTP Message Analysis Agent, a Contact Trust and Pattern Recognition Agent and a URL Analysis Agent. Each agent looks at a part of an incoming SMS. A LangGraph-based Coordinator Agent brings the agents together combines their results and outputs a label of Safe, Suspicious or Scam along with a risk score. The system first cleans messages and creates semantic embeddings for similarity-based threat detection. A MongoDB community database uses vector search to find messages that're semantically similar to known scam patterns. If the message matches known harmful patterns, the system doesn't have to analyze it. New messages go through the LangGraph multi-agent pipeline. Security controls keep the threat data trustworthy. In addition the system uses Explainable AI to give users an explanation of why a message is determined to be suspicious. the app can suggest steps that users can take, for instance, refraining from clicking on links or blocking the sender, which can help them make better security decisions.

papers.title: Agentic AI-Based Indian Legal Notice and Complaint Understanding with Source-Grounded Next-Step Guidance
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an Agentic AI-based architecture for understanding Indian legal notices and complaints using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Explainable AI (XAI). The proposed system aims to help ordinary citizens understand complex legal documents by extracting key information, identifying relevant legal provisions, and providing source-grounded explanations and next-step guidance. The architecture consists of an Orchestrator Agent and six specialized agents: Document Analysis, Legal Research, Summarization, Explainability, Next-Step Guidance, and Validation. It combines BM25 keyword search with FAISS dense-vector retrieval and cross-encoder re-ranking to identify relevant Indian statutes and legal references. The proposed generation component uses a LoRA-adapted LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct model. The system emphasizes traceability, factual grounding, and validation to reduce unsupported legal claims. It is intended to assist users in understanding legal documents and does not replace professional legal advice. This paper presents the proposed architecture and methodology, along with illustrative hypothetical case studies. Implementation and empirical evaluation remain future work.

papers.title: A Managed Database-as-a-Service Platform for Scientific Computing
papers.abstract: Scientific computing at HPC facilities increasingly relies on database infrastructure across a growing range of workloads: vector search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), structured analytics, and AI-driven knowledge discovery over community corpora spanning documentation, experimental datasets, simulation outputs, and literature collections. These corpora are inherently shared facility resources, serving researchers, facility support staff, and AI agents across projects and institutions. Yet the supporting infrastructure remains built per project: each team provisions, configures, and operates its own database instance, with no facility-level registry, no shared identity layer, and no uniform interface for discovering or accessing the databases hosted across the facility. Commercial cloud platforms have addressed analogous needs through managed Database-as-a-Service offerings (e.g., Amazon RDS, Snowflake, Pinecone). However, these solutions do not transfer cleanly to scientific computing: they rely on proprietary identity systems, cannot directly access facility filesystems, and incur substantial data egress costs. We are building the missing piece: a managed database platform that lives inside the HPC facility, developed and evaluated on ALCF Polaris. One federated sign-in (Globus) brings a researcher — or an AI agent acting on their behalf — to every database the facility hosts, through a web UI, a scriptable API, or the Model Context Protocol. Governance, catalog, and access control are handled once by the platform and inherited by every project by default. The central design choice is scaling, native to HPC. Each workload is decomposed into its resource-consuming stages, and each stage can be scaled independently across nodes. As one representative example, a vector-search workload scales GPU-based embedding generation and search-index serving independently across nodes, reaching 5,197 queries/sec on 8 nodes (4.3× single-node) on ALCF Polaris and still climbing at maximum tested concurrency. Governance adds modest overhead at single-user load and becomes negligible under concurrency. In an end-to-end RAG pipeline built on this workload, retrieval contributes under 2% of total latency — the bottleneck has moved entirely to LLM generation. The same decomposition pattern is designed to extend to other workload types as additional engine adapters are integrated. The talk presents what changes when scientific data services are native to the facility: who can use them, what AI agents become capable of, and how a single platform can replace per-project infrastructure across an entire lab. We will share the design tradeoffs, what the scaling numbers mean for facility capacity planning, and the next stage of the design — co-locating the database service with model-inference services and scaling both on demand against shared facility resources, planned for the coming year. We invite peer facilities to adopt the platform and collaborate with us on a unified, cross-facility scientific data service.

papers.title: Lossless Compression of Proximity Graph Indexes for Efficient Approximate Nearest Neighbors Search
papers.abstract: Graph-based Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexes, such as HNSW, are the backbone of modern vector search. However, their massive memory footprint creates a severe infrastructure bottleneck. While vector quantization is widely adopted to reduce the memory required to store data vectors, the graph's edge structure increasingly dominates total memory usage. Compressing these adjacency lists for online search presents a critical system challenge: because decompression occurs during query processing, i.e., while navigating the graph, memory savings cannot come at the expense of query latency. In this paper, we present a compression technique explicitly tailored for live HNSW routing. By applying offline graph permutations to artificially induce structural locality, we enable the use of SIMD-accelerated integer compressors, such as Stream VByte, for rapid on-the-fly decompression. Evaluated across diverse real-world workloads, we significantly outperform the current state of the art in both compression ratio and query latency. Our experimental results show that we achieve compression ratios up to 52.7% with negligible penalties in latency compared to the uncompressed baseline. Furthermore, our technique has been effectively deployed in production at eBay, achieving up to 44.3% reduction in edge storage with no degradation in query latency.

papers.title: On Worst-Case Guarantees for Graph-Based Nearest-Neighbor Search
papers.abstract: Graph-based nearest neighbor search algorithms like HNSW, DiskANN, NSG, and others have surged in popularity in recent years due to their excellent empirical performance in comparison to space-partitioning methods like IVF data structures and Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH). However, in contrast to LSH and related methods, obtaining strong worst-case theoretical guarantees for graph-based search has proven challenging. In this paper, we prove a strong lower bound that helps explain the lack of progress towards such guarantees. We show that no standard graph-based method (any that runs a variant of greedy search on a flat or hierarchical graph) can achieve sublinear query time for approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space, even for an arbitrarily large approximation factor. On the other hand, we prove that sublinear query time is possible if we allow for Steiner points in the search graph. We obtain bounds comparable to LSH, showing e.g., that graph-based search with Steiner points can solve $c$-approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space with query time $\tilde{O}(n^{1/(c-1)})$. We complement this result with initial experiments exploring how Steiner points can be incorporated into practical graph-based methods.

papers.title: Fast Sparse $α$-Navigable Graph Construction with Improved Resource Augmentation
papers.abstract: Graph-based nearest neighbor search methods, which run greedy search on a directed graph over the data points, have surged in popularity in recent years. A common goal is to construct a search graph with the $α$-navigability property, which ensures that greedy search returns provably good approximate nearest neighbors and converges in few iterations. Increasing $α\geq 1$ improves accuracy and convergence rate, but requires more edges, which increases both space and search time. This tradeoff has motivated the study of algorithms for constructing a sparsest $α$-navigable graph for a given set of points. For any point set and any distance function, we show how to compute an $α$-navigable graph with at most $O(\log n)$ times as many edges as the sparsest $(1+\varepsilon)α$-navigable graph, in $O(n^ω\log(Δ)/\varepsilon)$ time, where $ω< 2.372$ is the matrix multiplication exponent and $Δ$ is the aspect ratio of the input. This improves on Khanna, Padaki, and Waingarten (SODA 2026), who achieve the same runtime but are only competitive with the sparsest $2(1+\varepsilon)α$-navigable graph. Since sparsity often increases rapidly with $α$ (typically $α\leq 1.1$), their bound can be significantly weaker. Previously, the best algorithm competing with the sparsest $(1+\varepsilon)α$-navigable graph required $\widetilde{O}(n^{2.5})$ time. Our techniques also extend to constructing sparse $τ$-monotonic graphs, another popular target in nearest neighbor search. Finally, we give a fine-grained complexity analysis suggesting that improving the $O(n^ω)$ running time is unlikely, or would require a very different approach. It is based on hardness results for problems related to verifying whether a graph is navigable, a topic of independent interest.

papers.title: Fast Approximate Line Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.abstract: Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search, which retrieves vectors close to a given query vector, is a fundamental operation in vector databases. However, emerging applications, such as selecting source images for photo-based animation and video synthesis, may require matching content while allowing a query-specified aspect contrast, such as an illumination change, to vary; a single query point does not directly express this requirement. In this paper, we study approximate line nearest neighbor (LANN) search, where an infinite query line removes the distance contribution along a specified direction while database records remain points. Prior approaches focus on top-$1$ search only for LANN and can incur high construction costs. Converting LANN into ordinary point ANN search through dimension lifting substantially increases index construction and query costs, while direct search on a proximity graph built for ordinary point ANN search can miss distinct regions close to a line. To address these issues, we propose LinePG, which enhances an existing proximity graph with pair edges to facilitate navigation between separated near-line regions. To find these pair edges efficiently, we first generate region pairs with spatial or graph separation, and near a line. We then score edges between the selected region pairs to guide the point endpoint selections. We conduct extensive performance studies and confirm the accuracy and efficiency of LinePG in comparison with the baseline approaches.
