papers.title: RAG-Based MCA AI Agent for Document-Grounded College Information Assistance Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Vector Search and a Locally Hosted Large Language Model
papers.abstract: This paper presents the design and implementation of a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based MCA AI Agent for document-grounded question answering over college and student policy documents. The system uses PyMuPDF for PDF text extraction, approximately 1000-character chunks, Nomic-Embed-Text for generating 768-dimensional embeddings, and Pinecone for semantic vector search. At query time, the system retrieves the three most relevant document chunks and provides them as context to Llama 3.2 running locally through Ollama. A React.js frontend and FastAPI backend provide the conversational interface. The paper describes the system architecture, methodology, implementation, document-refresh workflow, and practical deployment considerations, including stale vectors and local inference latency. It also outlines an evaluation framework for comparing a standalone LLM with the proposed RAG pipeline using retrieval relevance, answer correctness, faithfulness, and latency. The current work is presented as a system implementation and preliminary study. A controlled quantitative evaluation has not yet been completed, and no numerical accuracy improvement is claimed. papers.title: VecForge: A Local-First Hybrid Vector Database with Persistent Agent Memory and Order-Preserving Grover-Inspired Reranking
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented applications and AI assistants need a vector store that runs inside the user's own process, keeps data encrypted on disk, combines semantic and keyword retrieval, and remembers information across conversations. This paper presents VecForge 2.0, an embedded Python vector database built for these needs. One SQLite file, optionally encrypted with SQLCipher, holds documents, vectors, metadata, access keys, agent sessions and index snapshots. Queries fuse FAISS dense search with an incremental BM25 index, and namespace and deletion constraints apply inside both indexes. A memory layer, served over the Model Context Protocol, ranks memories by relevance, importance and recency. The paper also proves that the Grover-inspired reranker of the previous release applies only the diffusion half of Grover's algorithm, so it can only keep or reverse a ranking, and replaces it with an O(N) closed form of the full algorithm that preserves order. Eighteen experiments evaluate every feature. On the SciFact benchmark, hybrid fusion reaches an nDCG@10 of 0.707, against 0.645 for dense search, 0.665 for BM25 and 0.681 for reciprocal rank fusion. Compared with the previous release, in-index constraints raise recall in small namespaces from 0.5% to 100%, incremental indexing makes insertion 183 times faster, and snapshots make reopening 9 to 17 times faster, while encryption and access control add little cost. The evaluation also reports where the design falls short, including slow, highly selective filters and memory deduplication that confuses paraphrases with changed facts. A single local file can therefore serve both retrieval and long-term memory for AI agents.

papers.title: Retrieval Is the New Record System: A Retrospective Analysis of Open-Source Contributions to Vector Databases and Embedding Infrastructure Underpinning Clinical AI (2025-2026)
papers.abstract: Background. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) sits inside many clinical artificial intelligence (AI) prototypes. A language model answers from documents a retrieval layer selects first. If that layer returns the wrong documents, or returns nothing and reports success, the error starts before the model generates a word. Vector databases and embedding tools form that retrieval layer in most designs, so their defects count as health infrastructure defects. Purpose. This study analysed one contributor's public pull request (PR) record in vector database and retrieval projects. It asked three practical questions in sequence. What kinds of defects did the contributions address? What share of the work reached merge? Where did the process break down? Methods. On 21 October 2026 I extracted my full PR record through the GitHub API (author:rtmalikian): 213 PRs across 94 repositories (85 external projects and 9 of the author's own repositories). I defined a subset for vector databases and retrieval infrastructure: 39 PRs across 8 repositories. I coded each PR by status at extraction and read the review threads of seven cases in depth. Two cases from projects next to the subset, cocoindex-io/cocoindex and sentence-transformers, were read for comparison and kept out of the subset counts. Results. Of the 39 subset PRs, 13 merged, 18 were still open, and 8 closed unmerged. Among the 21 resolved PRs, 61.9% merged. Open PRs made up 46% of the subset, the highest share in any part of my record. The merged work clustered around one defect class: silent failure. Code accepted values it should have rejected, dropped errors in background threads, or hid missing data behind a normal response. The hardest case was a long-lived branch. pymilvus #3621 sat open from 20 June 2026 with 12 comments, merge conflicts, and a Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) gap on a sync commit. Conclusions. The code in this subset was rarely the slow part. Review time was. The fixes that landed shared one pattern: they made a system fail loudly, with an accurate message, at the point where bad data entered. A retrieval system that says "no record found" when it means "the index is corrupt" will mislead a clinician the way a silent defect misleads a developer.

papers.title: CoWalk: Cooperative Walks for Agentic Batch Queries on Disk-Resident Graphs
papers.abstract: Workloads such as query rewriting, deep research and group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) issue batches of semantically related vector queries. Existing disk-resident approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) systems process these queries independently. On three workloads, 31 to 67 percent of the I/Os of a batch fetch a page that another query of the batch has already fetched. A page cache shared by the batch removes these I/Os, yet it makes a single-thread search only $1.1$ to $1.2{\times}$ faster, because the search time goes to distance computation and the cache does not change the walk of any query. We present CoWalk, which runs the queries of a batch as cooperating walks on one thread. Every query keeps its own candidate list, a page is read once per batch, and the full-precision vector on every fetched page is ranked by every query of the batch. A query therefore reaches the target recall with a shorter candidate list, which computes fewer distances and issues fewer I/Os. At recall@10 of 0.95, CoWalk answers a batch on one thread $1.6$ to $1.9{\times}$ faster than the fastest per-query baseline and issues $2.8$ to $6.9{\times}$ fewer I/Os. On a server it serves $3.0$ to $6.9{\times}$ the throughput of that baseline at a similar batch latency.

papers.title: Adaptive Digital Consciousness: An Evolutionary Framework for Human Identity Preservation Using Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) have greatly changed the interaction between man and machines through natural-language reasoning, content generation, personalization, and interaction via agents. However, traditional LLM applications do not provide a unified mechanism for maintaining a long-term, structured, and identity-consistent representation of a person during long-time interaction. As shown in the recent studies of generative agents, long-term LLM memory, agentic memory, lifelong learning, and AI self-identity, these processes present essential capabilities that have been studied as separate components. This paper presents the Adaptive Digital Consciousness (ADC) framework as the theoretical architecture for computational representation of core features of human identity. The ADC framework proposes a system of structured representation of Digital DNA for personal knowledge, experience, preferences, values, and behaviors and connects it to multilayer memory, semantic embeddings, vector retrieval, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), LLM reasoning, adaptive learning, and autonomous agents. The framework also proposes the notion of identity constraints and the system of updating memory, consolidating it, handling conflicts, forgetting, maintaining privacy, consent, and security, as well as monitoring the origin of digital information. The goal of the study is not to replicate biological or subjective consciousness The research motivation, previous works, the system suggested, as well as memory and adaptation techniques, evaluation techniques, ethics and applications of the findings, drawbacks of the research and future research directions on this subject.

papers.title: Beyond Similarity Search: Knowledge Graph Metadata Enrichment for Enterprise Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: A key challenge of RAG systems is retrieving information from enterprise documents created by multiple teams over time, where it is not possible to enrich the information using the latest information and metadata available outside the scope of organizational documentation responsibility. We investigated whether using a knowledge graph to store metadata and frequently changing information would improve upon knowledge retrieval over similarity search over embeddings. To perform the experiment, we created a snapshot of the SEC EDGAR dataset for a quarter, comprising 167,050 filings from 10,511 companies and 508,714 embedded chunks of risk-factor text. To simulate the enrichment, we created a knowledge graph of 430,257 nodes and 561,144 edges carrying an accession number on every edge. To evaluate the gain obtained via a graph-based design, we evaluated three architectures: text-to-SQL over typed columns, dense-vector RAG with HNSW cosine search, and a two-stage GraphRAG design. All architectures share the same model and temperature to allow comparison. Results are scored programmatically by an LLM as judge over 20 questions divided across four categories, each question asked three times. GraphRAG solved 16 of 20 questions on all three attempts, compared to 10 for text-to-SQL and 3 for vector RAG. GraphRAG lost on structured aggregation queries. Vector RAG lost the single-document category it was expected to win, passing 3 of 15 where GraphRAG passed 15 of 15, because company attribution is not recoverable from cosine similarity at this scale. All six confident falsehoods in the benchmark were text-to-SQL conflating distinct people who share a surname, the failure that resolving identity to an identifier before reading any text prevents structurally; GraphRAG made none. We claim no advantage beyond this corpus, this model and this question set.

papers.title: ExtenGen: A Lightweight Shared Memory Layer for AI Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Modern software teams increasingly rely on AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex to write, review, and debug source code. However, each agent session begins without knowledge of earlier sessions, so that decisions, architectural context, and institutional knowledge distributed across GitHub issues, pull requests, and chat threads are not carried forward. Developers consequently re-explain the same background repeatedly, which consumes time and tokens and produces inconsistent answers across team members. This report presents ExtenGen, a lightweight, self-hostable shared memory layer for AI coding agents. ExtenGen is implemented as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes two tools, store_observation and recall_context, and it follows a five-stage pipeline of Capture, Embed, Store, Retrieve, and Inject. Captured text is converted into vector embeddings using the OpenAI text-embedding-3-small model and stored in PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension, while row-level security policies restrict every row to authorised organisations and users. At query time, a cosine-similarity search combined with an access-control filter returns the top-k most relevant authorised observations, which are merged into the agent's prompt. The lightweight version supports two ingestion sources, live MCP agent sessions and GitHub commit and pull requests, and is intended for small-team, self-hosted deployment. The project demonstrates Retrieval-Augmented Generation, vector similarity search, and multi-tenant access control in a single applied system and aims to reduce repeated context explanation and token usage.

papers.title: Spiking Neural Networks Are Harder to Steal: A Benchmark Study of Model Stealing Attacks
papers.abstract: Machine learning models deployed behind query interfaces expose more than their predictions, because an adversary can use those predictions to rebuild the model itself. Model stealing attacks (MSAs) exploit this exposure by training a surrogate model that replicates the decision behavior of a target through black-box queries alone, without access to its parameters or training data. These attacks are well characterized for conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs), yet spiking neural networks (SNNs) process information in a fundamentally different way. SNNs communicate through sparse, discrete spikes, and their outputs depend on membrane potentials that evolve over time rather than on a static mapping from input to output. This temporal mode of computation suggests that the decision behavior of an SNN may be harder to reconstruct from its responses. This work tests that possibility by benchmarking four representative MSAs, namely the Papernot, Tramèr, T-RND, and color perturbation attacks, against SNNs and their ANN counterparts on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10. Across every attack and dataset, SNNs prove consistently more difficult to steal. Surrogates of SNNs achieve 10% to 20% lower agreement with the target model and 15% to 25% lower adversarial transferability than surrogates of ANNs. We attribute this resistance to the way SNNs compute, as their spike-based and time-dependent dynamics yield decision boundaries that ANN-based surrogates struggle to approximate, even under large query budgets. These findings extend the known resilience of SNNs beyond attacks on training data to the replication of model functionality, strengthening the case for neuromorphic architectures in security-sensitive applications.

papers.title: Cumulative Memory Sizing and Asymmetric Latency Dynamics in Local Retrieval-Augmented Generation Pipelines (2026)
papers.abstract: This systems engineering paper models end-to-end memory allocation and pipeline execution latency in air-gapped, on-premises Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architectures. A persistent operational bottleneck in local AI deployment is isolating generator LLM capacity while neglecting the cumulative VRAM demands of concurrent neural pipeline components. Key research investigations include: Quantitative memory footprint modeling across dense multi-lingual embedding models (BAAI/bge-m3, Nomic Embed v1.5) and high-precision cross-encoder rerankers (bge-reranker-large) co-existing in GPU VRAM. Dynamic Key-Value (KV) cache memory scaling under retrieved-context injection across 4,000 to 32,000 token prompt buffers on 8B, 14B, 32B, and 70B open-weight architectures. Host system RAM consumption and cache behavior of in-memory Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) vector indexing (Qdrant, ChromaDB) operating with zero GPU VRAM consumption. Hardware sizing bounds establishing minimum viable GPU silicon thresholds (Single RTX 4090 24GB vs. Dual RTX 3090 48GB vs. Apple Silicon Unified Memory). For the complete architectural decision matrix, automated benchmark scripts, and production Python deployment blueprints, access the full publication at TechGuidePro:https://www.besttechguidepro.com/2026/10/local-rag-hardware-vram-sizing-guide.html

papers.title: Embeddings: The Map Without a Cartographer
papers.abstract: The essay starts from Antisthenes, the Socratic who rejected definitions and held that to know what a thing is one must place it among others, and follows that intuition up to embeddings: vectors that place linguistic units in a mathematical space learned from their uses. It explains the embedding matrix, the distributional analysis of Harris and Firth, word2vec and cosine similarity, the analogy king minus man plus woman landing near queen, the Leibnizian dream of a characteristica universalis, latent semantic analysis, GloVe, ELMo and BERT, the attention that redraws the map sentence by sentence, Sentence-BERT and CLIP, vector search and RAG systems. It closes with the strangest part: nobody drew this map or decided in advance what each axis means, the geometry appeared as a result of training, and a map excellent for navigating language may not tell us where the borders that matter in the world are.
